newsitem.title: UK: British Energy first half loss narrows.
newsitem.headline: British Energy first half loss narrows.

text.p: Nuclear power generator British Energy Plc Thursday reported a narrower loss for the first half and predicted that electricity prices would slow in the rest of the year.

The company, posting its first results since it went public in July, reported a pro forma pretax loss of 53 million pounds ($89 million) for the first half to Sept. 30, compared with a loss of 169 million pounds ($284 million) in the year-earlier period.
The firm also said it did not expect prices to keep going up as they did in the first half of the year.

"The prices in the summer period have been somewhat higher, but we don't expect that to continue through the winter, half-on-half. And we expect the year-end output to be roughly the same as last year," chief executive Robert Hawley said.

British Energy said its output surged 12 percent to 31.5 Terawatt hours in the first half, boosted by maintenanence outages at its competitors' plants. A Terawatt hour, the largest unit of measurement for electricity sales, represents one billion kilowatt hours.
British Energy's partly-paid shares slid one pence (1.6 cents) to 134.5 ($2.26) at midday GMT.

"The numbers were pretty much what we expected, perhaps a tad better," said Greig Middleton analyst David Campbell, adding that he did not expect the outlook for short-term electricity prices to hurt the company's stock.

"It's had an extremely good run, and we would anticipate possibly a bit of a pause for breath. I wouldn't be surprised if after market consideration (of the results), the share price continues to go ahead," he said.
The firm also said it agreed to supply electricity to Southern Electric Plc for up to 15 years, expanding the companies' existing relationship.
Hawley declined to give financial details, but he did say the deal would increase British Energy's sales to Southern, which amounted to 6.5 Terawatt hours last year.
"The advantage is it gives us a degree of longer-term price stability which hedges against the uncertainty in pool prices," Hawley said.
Hawley said British Energy was talking to other electricity companies about similar deals.
He added the company was focusing on increasing output and cost-savings at its existing power stations but would also consider joint ventures in Britain and investments overseas.
